reading.title: 16.2.1 Using Traditional Enumerations
paragraphs: An unscoped enumeration gives names to integral choices and introduces its enumerator names into the surrounding scope. A traditional unscoped enumeration introduces named values and permits certain implicit conversions that can be convenient in older interfaces. It improves readability over raw numeric literals, but its names and conversion behavior can also create collisions or accidental mixing with unrelated integers.

For a small teaching example, offline, ready, and failed are clearer than zero, one, and two because they state the domain choices. The important improvement is the meaning carried by the names. A comment mapping numbers to states is weaker because the comment and code can diverge independently.

Do not assume that an enumeration validates external input by itself. Reading an integer from a file and casting it to an enumeration can produce a value that does not correspond to an accepted named state. Validate the external code before treating it as a domain choice.

An enumeration’s underlying representation is also not automatically a stable protocol specification. If a file or network format uses numeric state codes, define the mapping explicitly and version it as needed. Reordering declarations or adding a value should not accidentally redefine persisted data.

topics.summary: A scoped enumeration such as enum class State { offline, ready, failed }; keeps its names qualified and does not implicitly convert to an integer. State::ready therefore communicates both the choice and its domain. Two unrelated scoped enum types cannot be casually compared as if their numeric encodings were interchangeable.

blocks.text: Not every numeric constant belongs in an enum. A voltage threshold is a quantity, not necessarily one of a closed set of named choices. Use constexpr values with units or domain types for quantities, and enumerations for alternatives. At protocol boundaries, document both the symbolic meaning and the encoded value so that a future change does not silently reinterpret stored data.

blocks.text: Magic numbers hide policy inside representation. A condition such as state == 2 forces the reader to remember a mapping. state == State::failed carries the interpretation directly. The same principle applies to named quantity limits, menu choices, and validation results.

blocks.text: Not every number needs an enumeration. A measured temperature varies across a numeric range and is not naturally a list of named alternatives. A threshold is often a named constant; a small exclusive set of modes is often an enumeration. Choose the abstraction from the domain rather than converting every literal into a different kind of ceremony.

blocks.text: Be careful with casts at external boundaries. A cast expresses a conversion, not an approval. A parser should map accepted text or numeric codes to named states and reject unsupported input. That mapping can return a success flag and commit to an output state only after validation, following the candidate pattern from Chapter 11.

blocks.text: When logging a state, use a stable label function so the representation is consistent across call sites. Centralizing the mapping also gives tests one place to check every accepted alternative.

This distinction becomes the central topic of the next chapter. Public aggregate fields are convenient for transport and parsing; a class with a restricted interface can protect a stronger invariant after the candidate has been validated.

topics.title: Review and solution reasoning
topics.summary: Why is a struct not automatically a valid domain object? The language can create its members even when their combination violates application rules. Validation or construction policy must establish those rules.

cards.question: Why is a struct not automatically a valid domain object?
cards.answer: The language can create its members even when their combination violates application rules. Validation or construction policy must establish those rules.

cards.question: Why prefer enum class for new discrete choices?
cards.answer: It keeps names scoped and strengthens the type boundary against accidental mixing. Explicit conversions still require validation.

cards.question: Why not dump the struct’s raw bytes to a file?
cards.answer: Its in-memory representation can contain padding and nonportable member state, including string internals. A file format needs an explicit field representation.

cards.question: Why test a state absent from the sample vector?
cards.answer: Supported behavior extends beyond one fixture. Every named alternative needs coverage even when the initial demonstration does not use it.
